catalog_quote: Phonologically, Tiddim Chin has three contrastive tones with relatively complex tone sandhi, as well as several intonation patterns. ... As shown in Table 3, Tiddim Chin has three distinctive tones: a rising tone, a level tone, and a falling tone. The pitch of each tone varies according to vowel length and the sonority of a syllable-final consonant. ... 2.2 Syllable structure Tiddim Chin's syllable structure can be reduced to (C1) (V1) V2 (V3) (C2) / T, where C1 represents an onset consonant, V represents a vowel, C2 represents a coda consonant, and T represents a tone. Each syllable consists of a vowel and may include an onset and a coda. A majority of Tiddim Chin morphemes are phonologically monosyllabic (e.g., nê¹ "eat"), though a few show a disyllabic combination of two monosyllabic structures (e.g., pa³tâu³ "nervous"). ... new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Katsura 1964, p. 30 ( lines 135-152 and 171-174): the compiler reported no tone/accent terms in the scanned, but the paper explicitly describes Tiddim Chin tonemes (トネーム) with three types, 平板型 level, 上昇型 rising, 下降型 falling (examples ta:i 'flee' level vs ta:i 'scold' rising; sun 'stab' and su:n 'afternoon' falling), and says the missionary romanisation marks none of them; §3 says the phoneme and toneme system was worked out from a ~600-word list. This is a tone statement, not a stress statement, so it changes the per-work reading (none found -> tone language, no stress statement) but not the relation to the catalog (silent). No work marked silent says anything about word stress or accent.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: every fragment of the deciding quotation and the domain quote is present verbatim (modulo curly quotes/line wraps) at the stated pages in the Otsuka 2014 text we hold layer, and the sketch indeed never mentions stress/accent. Deciding source: a 2014 first-hand grammar sketch (33 pp, 4-pp phonology) — modern and reliable for 'three lexical tones, obligatory T in the syllable template, tone sandhi', and the tonal classification is independently confirmed by Ostapirat 1998 (downloaded now, p.235) and by the Henderson-derived tone marking in VanBik 2009; nothing found suggests word stress (the only contrary claim on record is an uncited AI-encyclopedia page already flagged on verification). So the classification 'tonal, no stress rule stated, domain not stated by the source' is safe and needs no reclassification. It is not, however, resting on the best available description: Henderson 1965 (172-pp OUP monograph) and Cin

sources.citation: Ostapirat, Weera. 1998. Tiddim Chin tones in historical perspective. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 21(1): 235-248. doi:10.32655/ltba.21.1.06
sources.quote: 'Tiddim Chin shows three tones in smooth syllables (syllables ending with sonorants and vowels): rising, level and falling, which are numbered by Henderson (1965) as tones 1, 2 and 3 respectively. Long checked syllables ... also occur with these three tones. Short checked syllables only occur with a low level tone, which has been considered to be an allotone of tone 3.' No mention of word stress/accent anywhere (a full-text search for stress/accent scanned: 'stress'/'accent'/'promin' occur only in non-prosodic senses).

sources.citation: [not in 'works'; already held by the project] Singh, Arambam Sadananda. 2018. A Descriptive Grammar of Sukte (Salhte). PhD dissertation, Assam University. Chapter 3, Phonology, pp. 23-74.
sources.note: Describes Sukte (Salhte), a Northern Kuki-Chin variety of Manipur closely related to Tedim (Katsura 1964 lists Sokte as a dialect of the Tiddim area); it is not the Tiddim/Tedim variety the catalog entry names. Even as a near relative it offers no stress statement.

sources.citation: [not in 'works'; already held by the project] Cing, Zam Ngaih. 2017. A descriptive grammar of Tedim Chin. PhD dissertation, North-Eastern Hill University (Shillong). Chapter 2, Phonology, pp. 24-68.
sources.note: Compatible with the catalog's empty rule: a full modern grammar of the language describes it as a three-tone language and makes no word-stress statement at all. Describes Tedim Chin as spoken in Manipur (India); the tone summary of Henderson (1965) on p. 48 says Henderson postulated three tones, High, Mid, Low, with low rising, level and high falling pitch.

sources.citation: [not in 'works'; already held by the project] VanBik, Kenneth. 2009. Proto-Kuki-Chin: A Reconstructed Ancestor of the Kuki-Chin Languages. STEDT Monograph 8. Berkeley: University of California.
sources.note: Nothing that would fill the catalog's empty rule; at most a hint (shared across Kuki-Chin, not specific to Tiddim) that non-root prefix syllables are unstressed and tone-reduced. Cites Henderson 1965:88 for Tiddim tone data.

sources.citation: VanBik, Kenneth. 2009. Proto-Kuki-Chin: A Reconstructed Ancestor of the Kuki-Chin Languages. STEDT Monograph 8. Berkeley: STEDT.
sources.quote: Comparative reconstruction; Tedim treated as a tone language (tones marked by numerals after Henderson); 'stress'/'accent' occur only as lexical glosses (e.g. *ʔuar 'emphasize, stress'). Silent on word stress.
sources.locator: a full-text search for stress/accent; Tedim data cited from Henderson 1965:88, Bhaskararao 1996, Khoi Lam Thang 2001
